sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match, one word or complete the table).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Stock is measured at a ______ of time. (b) Flow is measured over a ______ of time.
questions.answer:
(a) point
(b) period
(Capital is a stock; capital formation is a flow.)

questions.q: State True or False: (a) Roads constructed by the government are production. (b) Purchase of a tractor by a farmer is consumption.
questions.answer:
(a) True.
(b) False — a tractor adds to the farmer's capital stock, so it is investment (capital formation) for production, not consumption.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Capital formation is done by refraining from present ______. (b) Saving kept idle at home ______ (does / does not) lead to capital formation.
questions.answer:
(a) consumption
(b) does not

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Production is the making of goods and ______. (b) Labour and capital get ______ and interest respectively.
questions.answer:
(a) services
(b) wages

questions.q: Give one word: (a) Payment for the services of land. (b) Reward of the entrepreneur.
questions.answer:
(a) Rent.
(b) Profit.

questions.q: State True or False: (a) A teacher teaching in a school is production. (b) Growing vegetables in a kitchen garden is not production.
questions.answer:
(a) True — a service is produced.
(b) False — it creates utility, so it is production.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What are factor incomes? Name them.
questions.answer:
Factor incomes are the payments received by the owners of the factors of production for their productive services.
Land gets rent, labour gets wages, capital gets interest and the entrepreneur gets profit.

or.q: What is meant by the production process?
or.answer: Production is the creation of utility. In the production process the producer combines land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship with raw materials to turn them into goods and services that satisfy wants.

questions.q: Explain consumption as a basic economic activity.
questions.answer:
Consumption is the use of goods and services for the direct satisfaction of individual or collective wants, such as a household buying food, clothes, a cycle or a doctor's service.
It is the goal of production.

questions.q: In what two ways is production disposed of?
questions.answer: Production is used for (1) consumption, the direct satisfaction of wants, and (2) capital formation, the part not consumed that is added to the stock of machines, buildings and so on to expand future production.

questions.q: What are factor payments?
questions.answer:
Factor payments are what a firm pays the owners of factors for their services: rent to landlords, wages to workers, interest to owners of capital and profit to the entrepreneur.
For the owners, the same payments are factor incomes.

questions.q: Distinguish between fixed capital and working capital.
questions.answer:
Fixed capital is used in production for many years, e.g. machines, tractors and buildings.
Working capital is used up in a single round of production, e.g. raw materials such as yarn, seeds and fertilisers.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the four factor incomes.
questions.answer:
(1) Rent: paid to the landlord for the services of land.
(2) Wages: paid to labourers for their physical or mental work.
(3) Interest: paid to the owners of capital, e.g. a bank that lends money to buy a tractor.
(4) Profit: earned by the entrepreneur for organising production and bearing risk.

questions.q: How does saving lead to capital formation? Is all saving capital formation?
questions.answer:
Income not spent on consumption is saved and deposited in banks, which lend it to producers to buy machines, buildings and other capital goods. This addition to the capital stock is capital formation.
Not all saving is capital formation: money saved and locked up at home is idle, so no capital is formed.

questions.q: 'The larger the surplus, the larger the productive capacity of the economy.' Explain.
questions.answer:
The surplus is the part of production not consumed.
It is invested in capital goods such as plant, machinery and buildings, which is capital formation.
A larger surplus means more capital goods, so the economy can produce more in future.

questions.q: What are the functions of an entrepreneur?
questions.answer:
(1) Brings land, labour and capital together in the right proportion.
(2) Decides what and how much to produce and how much to spend on factors.
(3) Bears the risk and uncertainty of production.
(4) Pays rent, wages and interest, arranges the sale of output and earns profit.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the three basic economic activities and show how they are inter-related.
questions.answer:
(1) Production is the creation of utility by combining land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship to make goods and services.
(2) Consumption is the use of goods and services for the direct satisfaction of wants.
(3) Capital formation is the surplus of production over consumption that is added to the stock of capital goods.
Inter-relation: more production allows more consumption and more capital formation; more capital formation raises future production; rising consumption shows a higher standard of living. Together they take the economy towards development.

questions.q: Describe the four factors of production.
questions.answer:
(1) Land: a gift of nature — plains, mountains, plateaus, minerals and forests. It is limited and immobile.
(2) Labour: human effort, physical or mental, skilled or unskilled.
(3) Capital: man-made aids such as machines, tools and buildings. It raises the efficiency of land and labour. Fixed capital lasts many years; working capital is used up.
(4) Entrepreneurship: organises the other factors, takes decisions, bears risk and earns profit.

questions.q: Explain the types of occupations or economic activities and their components.
questions.answer:
Activities can be grouped by the basic economic activity they perform:
(1) Production activities create goods and services. They include agriculture and allied activities, manufacturing, and services such as teaching, transport and banking.
(2) Consumption activities are households buying and using goods and services to satisfy wants.
(3) Capital formation activities are saving and investing in machines, buildings, roads and wells.
In every occupation, factors earn rent, wages, interest and profit.
